13-057.r: India's imports in 2004-05 (descending share) → Fuel > Capital goods > Gold and silver > Chemicals; same order in 2022-23.

13-058.r: 2001-02: crude and petroleum products about 27% (27.2%) of India's imports (true); exports fell (–1.6%), did not rise 10%; only statement 1 correct.

13-059.r: India's imports by value (94-95 figures) → Petroleum > Capital goods > Pearls and precious stones > Chemicals > Iron and steel; by 2021-22 chemicals moved above pearls.

13-060.r: Biggest LNG supplier to India → Qatar (14.7 bcm of India's 28.4 bcm LNG imports in 2022), then UAE and USA.

13-061.r: West Texas Intermediate (WTI) → a grade of crude oil; one of three major oil benchmarks, with Brent and Dubai crude.

13-062.r: Haldia Port (West Bengal) imports fertilisers, foodgrains, coking coal, petroleum, iron and steel, machinery and general cargo.
13-062.c: Book gives no single answer: Haldia imports petroleum, iron and steel and machinery, so (b), (c) and (d) all fit.

13-063.r: Import procedure begins with the Indent (the import order), placed after foreign exchange is arranged through a Letter of Credit.

13-064.r: Letter of Credit → produced by the importer, through the importer's bank (Issuing Bank), promising payment to the exporter against stipulated documents.

13-066.r: Largest share in India's exports (2004-05 and now) → manufactured goods (71.2% in 2020-21; 58.9% in 2022-23).

13-067.r: Rising share of manufactured goods in exports (75.5% in 1992-93 to 78.0% in 1994-95) → best sign of structural transformation towards modernisation.

13-068.r: Highest export item from India (2017 and now) → engineering goods (US$ 112102 million in 2021-22), ahead of agriculture, chemicals and textiles.

13-069.r: Largest export items: Readymade Garments and Gems & Jewellery in the question period (per explanation); at present Engineering goods has the highest value and share.
13-069.c: Printed answer (a) Engineering Goods and Tea; the explanation says Readymade Garments and Gems & Jewellery (d) led in the question period.

13-072.r: Largest export earner: Gems and jewellery in the question period; among the given items, agricultural and allied products lead in recent years (14.3% in 2020-21).
13-072.c: Printed answer (a) uses recent data; the explanation says (b) Gems and jewellery was correct for the question period.

13-075.r: Gems and jewellery share in India's exports → about 18% (2010 statistics); 9.3% of commodity exports in 2021-22.

13-076.r: Among iron, tea, textile and rubber → India earns the most foreign exchange from textiles (US$ 36686 million in 2022-23).

13-077.r: India's high diamond export earnings → expertise in cutting and polishing imported diamonds; India exports 75% of the world's polished diamonds (GJEPC).

13-078.r: Arid and semi-arid Middle East countries export fruits, dry fruits and palm oil to India.

13-079.r: Tiruppur (Tamil Nadu), 'Manchester of South India' → huge exporter of knitted garments (hosiery); 90% of India's cotton knitwear export.

13-080.r: India → third largest exporter of textiles and apparels in the world; second largest producer of MMF fibre after China (Ministry of Textiles, 2022-23).

13-081.r: Largest importer of Indian textiles → USA (29% in 2022-23), then Bangladesh, UK and UAE, Germany.

13-082.r: Top exporting State in 2007-08 and 2008-09 → Maharashtra; now Gujarat leads (33.12% in 2022-23), Maharashtra second.

13-083.r: 2001-02 (book): A false, exports did not fall by 2.17%; R true, iron and steel, coffee, textiles and marine products had negative export growth.

13-084.r: India's exports → destination: Iron ore → Japan (from Bailadila); Leather goods → Russia; Tea → UK; Cotton fabrics → USA.

13-085.r: India's largest steel export destination in 2003-04 → China (23.0% share); in 2023-24 → Italy, then Belgium.

13-086.r: India's largest leather export market → USA (19.13%, April 2023 to March 2024), then Germany and UK.

13-087.r: India's exports grew about 18% in 1994-95; in 2021-22 they rose 44.6% to about US$ 422 billion.

13-088.r: Highest export growth among 2002-03 to 2005-06 → 2004-05 (30.8%, Economic Survey 2007-08).

13-089.r: India became the world's largest rice exporter in 2015, replacing Thailand; still top in 2022-23, followed by Thailand, Vietnam, Pakistan.

13-090.r: World's largest tea exporter → Kenya; order in 2021 and 2022: Kenya > China > Sri Lanka > India.
13-090.t: Don't pick India or Sri Lanka: Kenya leads tea exports; India is only fourth.

13-091.r: Switzerland → world's largest gold exporter by value (USD 101 billion, 2022): true; but not second in gold reserves (top: Australia, Russia, South Africa).

13-092.r: Cultured pearl production → important cottage industry of Japan (pioneer Kokichi Mikimoto, Akoya oyster).

13-093.r: Long staple cotton: USA was the largest producer and exporter in the question period; now India is the top producer and USA the top exporter.

13-094.r: Largest services foreign exchange earner (2007-08, 2008-09 and now) → IT-Software services; IT services are over 51% of IT-BPM.

13-095.r: Indian software exports grew over 50% a year since 1995-96 (CAGR 57% in IX Plan) as firms were cost-effective with international quality; A and R true, R explains A.

13-096.r: Question period: software exports grew at about 60% CAGR and the software industry about 28% in 2001-2002 (both correct); 2022-23 software exports US$ 185.5 billion.

13-097.r: Foreign visitors watching the XIX Commonwealth Games in India → an export (tourism earnings are an invisible export).

13-098.r: Invisible export → export of services (tourism, banking, insurance, software, finance); no goods are involved.

13-099.r: Entrepot trade → goods imported for re-export, with no processing and no customs duty (trans-shipment port).

13-100.r: Tariff (tax on imports) raises import prices → reduces the volume of trade; now used mainly to protect domestic industry.

13-101.r: Duty drawback → refund to exporters of customs and excise duties paid on inputs used to make export goods (refund of import duty).

13-102.r: Slow growth of India's exports → high price, foreign competition, low quality goods: all of these; India's share was 1.8% of global exports in 2022.

13-103.r: Exim Policy of 1992 → 5 years; FTP 2015-20 extended to 31 March 2023; FTP 2023 dropped the five-year tradition for a long-term focus.

13-104.r: Exim Policy 2002-2007 aimed at least 1% (not 10%) of global trade by 2007; EHTP units could sell in DTA only up to 50% of FOB value.

13-105.r: Foreign Trade Policy of the question period → 2004-2009 (five years); FTP 2023 adopts a long-term focus instead.

13-106.r: Foreign Trade Policy 2004-09 (August 2004): aim to double India's share of global merchandise trade; stressed both development and employment; not 2005-10.

13-107.r: FTP 2004-09 target → raise India's share in world trade to 1.5% by 2009; FTP 2015-20 target: from 2% to 3.5% by 2019-20.

13-108.r: Foreign Trade Policy 2009-14 (Anand Sharma): double India's share of global trade by 2020; double exports by 2014; 15% growth till 2011, then 25%.

13-109.r: Registered exporters (ascending): Export House → Trading House → Star Trading House → Super Star; high export performance over many years → Star Trading House.

13-110.r: EXIM Policy 2002-07 was liberal and market-oriented; GATT/WTO helped liberalise the economy; both true but R does not explain A.

13-111.r: FTP 2009-14 → 21 'Towns of Export Excellence', including Panipat, Ludhiana, Tirupur and Madurai (none excluded); FTP 2023 added Faridabad, Moradabad, Mirzapur, Varanasi.

13-112.r: Closed economy → no trade with other economies: neither exports nor imports; fully self-sufficient.

13-113.r: Globalisation → growing interdependence of world economies; mainly free trade by dismantling barriers in international trade.

13-114.r: Globalisation of Indian economy → minimum possible restrictions on economic relations with other countries (free flow of goods, services, capital, people).

13-115.r: Globalisation includes lower import duties, no import licensing, free FDI flow; disinvestment of public sector equity is privatisation/liberalisation, not globalisation.

13-116.r: Globalisation pushed Indian firms to seek foreign investment and buy foreign ventures, and foreign firms to buy Indian ones; it did not create optimism among small entrepreneurs.

13-117.r: Cutting import duties on capital goods → key liberalisation tool (after 1991), helping local entrepreneurs upgrade technology for global markets; A and R true, R explains A.

13-118.r: First phase of liberalisation → 1991 New Economic Policy under Prime Minister P.V. Narsimha Rao.

13-119.r: Encouraging MNCs in India → promotes privatisation, globalisation and liberalisation: all of the above.
13-119.h: LPG: Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation all welcome MNCs.

13-120.r: After 1991: India's share in world exports rose (0.5% in 1990 to 1.8% in 2022); FDI and forex reserves rose; agriculture's share fell (about 30% to 17.6%).

13-122.r: Globalisation expanded trade and FDI inflows into India, but exports did not grow faster than imports (merchandise trade deficit kept rising).

13-123.r: Economic reforms in India began in 1991 amid a severe economic crisis: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.
